what: The header of the catalogue of texts by identifier: the version a project freezes. Declared BY HAND, for the same reason as the gate catalogue (gates/catalog.json) and the prompt corpus (prompts/catalog.json): a project starts and finishes with the same version of the method, so what it froze has to read back the same two years from now.

extracted_from.note: The texts are EXTRACTED from the prose of the method, not written here and not transcribed. This is the list of what each kind is read from, in every language the prose declares; if a text is not there, publication is refused.
extracted_from.steps: docs/<language>/ESCALERA_METODOLOGICA.md -- the heading of each step card
extracted_from.stations: docs/<language>/EVOLUTIVO_CORRECTIVO.md -- the heading of each station
extracted_from.rules: docs/<language>/ANEXO_HEURISTICAS.md -- the row of each rule
extracted_from.faces: docs/<language>/ANEXO_HEURISTICAS.md -- the row of each face of a rule that has faces, read with the same extractor as a rule
extracted_from.face_titles: the same row as the statement of the face: a face carries two texts, its statement and its short name, so it is two kinds

version_scheme.note: The recipe -- canonical form, algorithm, encoding, and the rule that raises the version -- is declared once, there, and the build uses the same implementation. This file only says which keys the fingerprint covers here, because the payload is a different one. One copy of each text.
version_scheme.what_is_covered: Everything the file says and everything it carries. `labels` is the payload; `counts` is the summary a tool uses to check it finished reading, and a summary of quantities that can lie is worse than no summary; `scope` is where the file declares what it leaves out and why, and a declaration of scope that an attacker can edit is a declaration that says nothing; `what` is where it states the reach of its own protection. The only keys outside are publication metadata, which a regeneration moves without changing a single text.

changelog.changed: First published version of the catalogue of texts. It closes the half that was missing from the gate catalogue since its first version: that file tells a consumer not to print its texts and to take them from its own catalogue instead, and the method published no catalogue to take them from, so the only machine-readable text was exactly the one it asked not to print. The instruction was right and impossible to obey. Coming in: the title of the twenty-four steps, the title of the eight normalisation stations and the statement of the forty-six rules of Annex H, in the eight languages the prose of the method declares -- seventy-eight identifiers per language, six hundred and twenty-four strings, every one of them EXTRACTED from the prose and none of them written or transcribed here. What stays out is declared in `scope` with the measurement that supports it: the evaluator vocabulary, which exists in one language only at the data layer, and the verification questions of a step, which are not the same list in the data and in the prose of the contract. The resource is UTF-8 and NOT pure ASCII, like the prompt corpus and for the same reason: the text of the prose travels verbatim, typographic punctuation included.

Two kinds enter, faces and face_titles, and with them the sixty strings of the two rules D-078 added. The gate catalogue now has rules with FACES -- a cut of the statement of a rule with an identifier of its own, so that a single one can be switched off -- and a consumer has to be able to print what it switched off: a report that says CQ-19.2 and nothing else is the opaque id with no catalogue behind it, which is exactly the defect this resource exists to close. A face carries two texts and is therefore two kinds, not one: its statement, like a rule, and its short name, like the title of a step -- the name is what a report prints next to the id, and the statement is what the reader needs in order to understand why. Both are EXTRACTED from Annex H of each language with the same extractor that already resolves the statement of a rule; not one string is written here, and the test that demands every string appear literally in the document it claims to come from covers them from the first day. What the count does: 24 step titles, 8 station titles, 48 rule statements and 6 faces counted twice, which is 92 ids per language and 736 strings over the eight languages the prose declares -- and every one of those figures is derived from the data and from the list of prose versions, not written in this file (D-067, D-077). What this version does NOT do: add a language, change a single text of the twenty-four steps, the eight stations or the forty-six rules that were already published, or widen what the scope leaves out (D-078, PND-065 to PND-068).

The thirty-two strings of CQ-21 and its three faces (D-087). One rule enters the gate catalogue with three faces, so the text catalogue carries four more statements and three more face titles per language: eight ids, thirty-two strings, extracted from the prose of each language like every other one. Nothing is written here: the test demands that every one of them appear LITERAL in the annex of the language it says it comes from, which is what keeps this resource from becoming a second version of the method. What does NOT change: the kinds, the scope, the exclusions and the derivation of the languages from languages.prose_versions.

The statements of CQ-22, CQ-23 and CQ-24 come in, plus the ten new faces -- the four of CQ-22, the three of CQ-23, the two of CQ-24 and CQ-21.4, which is the first face a published rule gained after entering -- extracted from the annex of the eight languages the prose declares, like every other string here. Nothing was written in this file and nothing was transcribed: a text that is missing in one language refuses the publication of the whole resource (D-089).

The statement of CQ-25 comes in, plus its four faces, extracted from the annex of the eight languages the prose declares, like every other string here. Nothing was written in this file and nothing was transcribed: a text that is missing in one language refuses the publication of the whole resource. The English dated note that the previous version left missing in the annex of that language was written in the same change, so the eight versions carry the same prose around the same rows (D-095).
